title: The Origin of the Flute
summary: Pathak ji's account of the flute's origin: wind sounding broken bamboo in the forest made the first single-note, 'god-made' flute; forest-dwellers copied it and cut holes; Śrī Kṛṣṇa set seven notes in it, earlier flutes giving three; later a fipple was added, easier to play but, he argues, limiting the tone.

blocks.text: Here Begins the Section on Making
Although learned men hold many views about its origin, in this scientific age my view is different from all of them, and reasoned.

blocks.verse:
स्वेच्छया वायुनाऽरण्ये बंशखण्डो निनाद्यते।
एक स्वरा स्वयं भूता बंशी सा देवनिर्मिता।।६।।
blocks.text: When a piece of bamboo in the forest is sounded by the wind of its own accord, that single-note, self-born flute is made by the gods.

That is: from whenever half-cut bamboos in the forest began to sound by themselves through the impact of the wind, from then the origin of the ekasvarā (single-note) flute should be reckoned, which we can call devanirmitā (god-made).

blocks.verse:
नररूपधरो भगवान् कृष्णः क्रीड़ां चिकीर्षयन्।
स्वराणाम् कल्पने वंशे सप्तानां कृत्वान् स्वयम्।।७।।
blocks.text: Lord Kṛṣṇa, taking human form and wishing to play, himself devised the seven notes in the bamboo.

In the same way, bamboos broken by the impact of the wind went on sounding for a long time, and they still do. Among them, broken bamboos of different lengths and widths have sometimes produced several nādas (musical sounds) at once. Curious forest-dwellers imitated them and began to play by blowing with the mouth. Then they made holes in it as they wished, and made it an instrument for folk songs. In the Vedas the name of the sage Tumburu comes up in connection with playing the flute.

Later, in the Dvāpara age, Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra gave the flute a special place in his childhood play and refined it further; he established the seven notes according to the śāstra, and used to play rāgas and rāginīs on it with skill.

Before this the flute had no separate mukharandhra (mouth-hole). Blowing from the natural opening alone, [players] drew three notes, which are described in the Vedas under the names udātta (raised accent), anudātta (lowered accent) and svarita (falling accent).

blocks.verse:
युगान्तरे तु संप्राप्ते मानवैर्लाधवेच्छया।
बंशीम् जिह्वावतीम् चक्रे कश्चिद् गीतविशारदः।।८।।
blocks.text: But when another age came, some master of song, because people wanted ease, made the Jihvāvatī (fipple flute).

Then, in the Kali age, some convenience-seeking scientific musician made a jibbhī (fipple) in it, which made it still easier. Even children began to play it. But science holds development in one hand and destruction in the other. So the sweetness that comes into the sound on the āḍī bansī (transverse flute) through practice of the lips is, on the flute with a fipple, limited and dependent, and to some extent even harmful to health. Because it is so easy, it sometimes gets broken in children's hands.
